newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries in London hold up despite dollar slide.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries in London hold up despite dollar slide.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were steady in London on Monday having held their own despite an overnight tumble in the dollar, analysts said.
The dollar slipped to 118.00 yen, its lowest level since late January, before recovering slightly. By 1050 GMT, it was trading at 118.67/77 yen.
A Treasuries trader at a French bank in London said weakness in the currency was often accompanied by lower Treasuries prices, but for now investors were looking to buy the long end.
"We have seen better buying in London by Japanese accounts which is possibly diversification trading," he said.
"Because the dollar fell, investors are buying dollar assets hoping the currency will appreciate again, so there has been better buying at the long end."
At 1050 GMT, the long bond was at 96-19 to yield 6.895 percent, unchanged from Tokyo, and versus 96.20 at New York's Friday close.
Two-year T-notes were at 100-08, unchanged from Tokyo and New York, while five-year paper was slightly higher at 100-14, compared with 100-13 in Tokyo and New York.

"Treasuries are holding a firm bid," the trader said. "(Japanese) life insurers have lost about six percent on the currency so they are looking to hedge their positions, but if the dollar was to break down even more we might see some liquidation."

He said the curve had steepened since Friday on front end buying after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments last Thursday were interpreted as reducing the likelihood of a rate increase at the May 20 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
"Arbitrage players have been buying back the front end and selling tens and bonds, helping the curve steepen a bit," he said.
Analysts said the swathe of U.S. data due this week were expected to be benign and encouraging for the Treasuries market.
U.S. April retail sales data are due on Tuesday, while the producer price index will be released on Wednesday.

Later in the week, April consumer prices and industrial production are due on Thursday and at the end of the week, the first of the May data, the Philadelphia Fed Survey and the preliminary University of Michigan sentiment survey will be published.
Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at BankAmerica in London, said the general background was cautiously optimistic but with a question mark hanging over the dollar.
"In general the impression is that this week's figures should be sufficiently soft that we are going to see at least domestic enthusiasm to buy Treasuries during the course of this week," he said.
"The pick of the data will be the producer price index on Wednesday and if that is as soft as we anticipate it will help convince the market that the Fed won't tighten next week," Hawkins said.
BankAmerica were expecting the data to come in flat on the month and for the core rate to be 0.1 percent higher.
June T-bond futures were at 100-07 in automated trade, unchanged from the Chicago settlement on Friday.
"We are pretty firmly entrenched in the 109-20 to 110-10 area," the trader said. "If it breaks up above 110-20 I would say we are in a bull market."
--Deepthi Wickremasinghe, Bonds Unit +44 171 542 4041
